- **HSE Ireland (2021) did not.** The government said on day one it would not pay. On 20 May the attackers posted a decryption key anyway; the HSE's IR provider validated it on 21 May. Even so, recovering all servers and 1,075 of 1,087 applications took until 21 September, and the review notes backups were only periodically copied to offline tape.

**MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment (2023)**, hit by the same crime group per reporting. Caesars' Form 8-K (a report to the SEC, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, on a major event) said the actor took a copy of its loyalty database and that it had taken steps to have the data deleted; it was [reportedly](https://www.theregister.com/2023/12/28/casino_ransomware_attacks/) paid about USD 15 million. MGM shut down systems and, per reporting, did not pay; its later 8-K estimated about USD 100 million of negative impact on Adjusted Property EBITDAR (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and rent, a casino-industry profit measure), mostly in Las Vegas in September.

blocks.code:
playbook: ransomware
severity: SEV1
trigger:
  - ransom note found, or files being encrypted on several hosts
  - EDR alert for shadow copy deletion or a known ransomware family
roles:
  incident_commander: on-call IR lead     # decides, does not type commands
  scribe: second on-call                  # keeps the incident log
  comms: communications on-call
  legal: general counsel + outside counsel on retainer
first_hour:
  - open the bridge on the out-of-band channel (phones, separate tenant)
  - capture memory and a disk image from a sample of affected hosts
  - isolate affected hosts with EDR; if whole subnets, cut at the switch
  - disable accounts seen in the attack; wipe nothing yet
  - confirm backups are offline and untouched; cut backup servers off
  - legal decides on law enforcement contact and starts the notice clocks
decision_points:
  - id: shutdown
    ask: could the spread reach safety systems or OT? stop operations?
    owner: CEO (anyone may stop work if safety is at risk)
  - id: ransom
    ask: can backups restore in time? was data stolen? sanctions check?
    owner: CEO with board and legal, after law enforcement input
  - id: notify
    ask: personal data hit (GDPR 72 h)? material for investors (8-K)?
    owner: legal
recovery:
  - rebuild domain controllers first, from a backup checked for IOCs
  - reset privileged credentials; krbtgt twice, 10+ hours apart
  - restore in business priority order; scan restored data for IOCs
exit:
  - no attacker activity through the agreed monitoring window
  - after-action review booked with all teams
blocks.caption: A ransomware playbook in YAML. Owners are named for each decision before the incident; the details are an example to adapt.

blocks.md: Do not read the casino pair as "paying works". As one threat analyst quoted by The Register put it, the incidents are not necessarily comparable: we do not know their scope or which systems and backups were hit. And paying did not stop Caesars' data theft or its notification duties.

blocks.question: A US company is considering paying a ransom. Under OFAC's 2021 advisory, which statement is correct?
options: Paying is legal as long as you did not know the group was sanctioned
Only the insurer is liable, never the victim
OFAC requires every victim to pay through the Treasury
Civil liability can be strict, so a payment to a sanctioned party can violate regulations even without knowledge; early law enforcement reporting and cooperation are significant mitigating factors
blocks.explain: The advisory says OFAC may impose civil penalties based on strict liability, and treats a complete, early report to law enforcement and ongoing cooperation as significant mitigating factors.

blocks.question: During the 2017 NotPetya outbreak, a victim pays the ransom. What happens, according to Kaspersky's analysis?
options: They get a working key within hours
Nothing useful: the installation ID was random, so the attackers had no way to produce a key for that disk
Only the master boot record is restored
The payment is automatically refunded
blocks.explain: Kaspersky found the installation ID that a real ransomware operator needs for key recovery was generated from random data. NotPetya was a wiper presented as ransomware.

lessons.title: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks

blocks.md:
Communication goes wrong in incidents more often than forensics does. NIST SP 800-61r3 sorts it into four kinds:

- **Coordination**: between the people and organisations doing the response.
- **Notification**: formally telling affected customers, employees, partners or regulators.
- **Public communication**: the press and the public.
- **Information sharing**: usually voluntary, for example telling your sector's **ISAC** (Information Sharing and Analysis Center) about the attacker's tactics so others can defend.

Internal updates go on a fixed rhythm over the OOB channel, to the people who need them, from the communications role, with facts and the time of the next update. NIST recommends regularly updating senior leadership on major incidents and having media procedures in advance.

**The clocks.** Several laws start a timer from a defined moment, and the moment is rarely "when the investigation is finished":

- **GDPR Article 33** (the EU General Data Protection Regulation): a controller must notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach *without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it*, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. Later notices must give reasons for the delay, and information may be provided *in phases*. A processor must tell the controller without undue delay. The HSE reported to Ireland's Data Protection Commissioner (DPC) on 15 May 2021, the day after the attack.

- **SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05** (US Securities and Exchange Commission rule of July 2023): a registrant (a company filing reports with the SEC, typically a listed company) must disclose a cybersecurity incident it determines to be **material** within **four business days of that determination**, which itself must be made without unreasonable delay. Disclosure can be delayed if the US Attorney General determines it would pose a substantial risk to national security or public safety.
- Sector and national rules add others (health, finance, critical infrastructure, US states). NIST notes that notification law changes often; legal keeps the list.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def gdpr_deadline(aware):              # Art. 33: 72 hours, calendar time
    return aware + timedelta(hours=72)

def sec_8k_deadline(material_day, holidays=()):
    d, left = material_day, 4          # Item 1.05: four business days
    while left:
        d += timedelta(days=1)
        if d.weekday() < 5 and d not in holidays:   # Mon-Fri only
            left -= 1
    return d

aware = datetime(2026, 3, 6, 16, 0)    # Friday 16:00: breach of EU data confirmed
print("GDPR report due:", gdpr_deadline(aware).strftime("%a %d %b %H:%M"))

material = datetime(2026, 3, 12).date()   # Thursday: board finds it material
print("8-K due by:     ", sec_8k_deadline(material).strftime("%a %d %b"))
blocks.caption: Deadline arithmetic for a synthetic case. GDPR counts calendar hours; Item 1.05 counts business days, so the weekend does not count. Public holidays would be passed in the holidays argument.

blocks.title: Two clocks in one week (synthetic case, days from Fri 6 March 00:00)

scenes.caption: Friday 16:00: the team confirms EU customers' data was accessed. The controller is now aware; the 72-hour clock starts.
Monday 16:00 is the deadline, weekend included. An initial notice with what is known, completed in phases, beats a perfect late one.
Thursday 12 March: the disclosure committee determines the incident is material. The SEC clock starts from that determination, not from discovery.
Four business days after Thursday is Wednesday 18 March (Fri, Mon, Tue, Wed); Saturday and Sunday do not count. The 8-K is filed by then.

blocks.md:
**In practice (2023).** MGM and Caesars both reported their incidents on Form 8-K in September 2023, before Item 1.05 disclosures were required, using other items. Caesars' filing described the social-engineering attack on an outsourced IT support vendor, the stolen loyalty database, free credit monitoring for all loyalty members and a dedicated incident response phone line, with individual notices to follow "on a rolling basis". MGM's October 8-K gave the estimated financial impact and the categories of customer data taken.

Customers want three things: what happened to *their* data, what you are doing, and what they should do (change a password, watch for phishing that uses the incident as a lure).
Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

blocks.question: A listed US company determines on a Thursday that an incident is material. With no holidays, what is the latest day to file the Item 1.05 Form 8-K?
options: The following Monday
The following Tuesday
The following Wednesday
Exactly 96 hours later, on Monday
blocks.explain: The rule counts four business days after the determination: Friday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Weekends are skipped, so it is not a 96-hour calendar clock like GDPR's 72 hours.

blocks.question: When does the GDPR Article 33 clock for notifying the supervisory authority start?
options: When the controller becomes aware of the personal data breach
When the investigation is complete
When the first customer complains
When the attacker publishes the data
blocks.explain: Article 33 says not later than 72 hours after having become aware of the breach, where feasible. Information that is not yet available may be provided in phases.

lessons.title: When the incident is not an attack: CrowdStrike, July 2024

blocks.md:
NIST's incident definition is about confidentiality, integrity and **availability**; an incident needs no attacker. In July 2024 a security product's update took millions of Windows machines down, and the organisations that recovered fastest were the ones that ran it like any other major incident: declare, scope, contain, recover, communicate, learn.

**What happened**, from CrowdStrike's root cause analysis (RCA). The Falcon sensor (CrowdStrike's EDR agent, which runs partly in the Windows kernel) receives *Rapid Response Content* through *channel files* interpreted by its content interpreter. A template type for detecting attacks via Windows interprocess communication defined 21 input fields, but the code calling the interpreter supplied only 20. Earlier content had used a wildcard for the 21st field, so the mismatch went unnoticed. On 19 July 2024 at 04:09 UTC, a new version of Channel File 291 used the 21st field for real; reading it went past the end of the input array, an out-of-bounds read in kernel code, and Windows crashed. The update was reverted at 05:27 UTC.

**Scale and recovery.** Microsoft estimated 8.5 million Windows devices were affected, under one percent of all Windows machines (per CISA's alert), concentrated in enterprises running critical services. Machines that pulled the file crashed at boot, usually before a fix could arrive (some got it after many reboots), so most needed hands-on work: boot into Safe Mode or the Windows Recovery Environment and delete the file matching `C-00000291*.sys`, or for virtual machines attach the disk to a repair VM ([Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2024/07/crowdstrike-fixes-start-at-reboot-up-to-15-times-and-get-more-complex-from-there/)). Disks protected by BitLocker needed their recovery keys first, a problem where the keys sat on servers that were also down. By 21 July Microsoft had released a USB-based recovery tool (per CISA's alert).

CISA's alert relayed CrowdStrike's confirmation that the outage was not caused by malicious cyber activity, and warned that threat actors were using it for phishing; CrowdStrike published lists of domains impersonating it.

scenes.caption: 04:09: Channel File 291 version with the bad template instances is released to sensors that are online.
Hosts that receive it crash, and crash again at each boot, because the sensor reads the file early. Most cannot fetch a fix before crashing again.
05:27: reverted. Per CrowdStrike, hosts that did not connect during the 78-minute window were not impacted; crashed ones stayed down, which is why recovery took days.
Customer IT declares, triages by business priority and fixes each machine by hand. BitLocker key access decides how fast.
Same day: fake fixes and look-alike domains appear. Communications must point staff to the one legitimate source of guidance.

blocks.prompt: The bad file was reverted 78 minutes after release. Why did many organisations still need days to recover?
blocks.reveal:
Because the crash happened at boot, before the sensor or any management tool could download the corrected file. Apart from the lucky ones that grabbed the fix after many reboots, affected machines needed someone (or a script on recovery media) to delete the file locally, and encrypted machines needed their BitLocker recovery keys first.

The recovery bottlenecks were all *preparation* items: an inventory of what was affected, recovery keys reachable when Windows servers are down, enough hands at each site, and runbooks for cloud VMs.

blocks.code:
# Preparation check, read-only: is there a recovery password for C:, and
# is it stored somewhere you can reach when every Windows PC is down?
manage-bde -protectors -get C:

# Same information as objects, for a fleet report
Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty KeyProtector |
  Select-Object KeyProtectorType, KeyProtectorId
blocks.caption: A read-only preparation check. Both commands list the protectors on drive C:, including the recovery password protector whose key you would need. Verify the keys are escrowed where you can read them during a Windows-wide outage.

blocks.md:
**What changed.** CrowdStrike's preliminary post-incident review committed to a staggered deployment of Rapid Response Content (canary hosts first, then wider rings) and to giving customers control over when and where such updates deploy. Its RCA lists the validation gaps: the content validator expected 21 inputs, and testing used wildcards for the 21st field.

For IR teams the lessons are general: any agent with kernel access and a fast update channel is a single point of failure; recovery tooling must not depend on the systems it recovers; and the playbook for "half the company's PCs will not boot" is worth having whether the cause is a wiper or a vendor.
Treat large non-malicious outages with the same machinery as attacks: incident commander, severity, OOB communications, a timeline and a blameless review. Attackers will use the confusion either way.

blocks.question: Why could CrowdStrike's revert at 05:27 UTC not fix machines that had already crashed?
options: The revert was only for Linux
Customers had to pay for the fix
Windows blocks all updates for 24 hours after a crash
The machines usually crashed at boot before they could download the corrected channel file, so most needed local intervention
blocks.explain: The faulty file was loaded early in boot, causing a crash before the sensor or management tools could fetch the fix. Recovery meant Safe Mode or recovery environment work on each machine, slowed by BitLocker keys.

blocks.question: Which preparation item would have most shortened recovery for a company whose BitLocker recovery keys were stored only in on-premises Active Directory, whose servers also crashed?
options: A faster internet connection
Keeping recovery keys escrowed in a place reachable during a Windows-wide outage (for example a separate, tested system or offline copy)
Disabling BitLocker permanently
Buying more EDR licences
blocks.explain: The keys were needed before any fix, and they sat on systems that were also down. Recovery dependencies must survive the failure you are recovering from.

lessons.title: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises

blocks.md:
An incident's value to the organisation comes from what changes afterwards. NIST r2 calls the lessons-learned step one of the most important and most often omitted parts of IR.

A **postmortem** (also *post-incident review* or *after-action report*) is a written record of what happened, its impact, the actions taken, the root and contributing causes, and follow-up actions with owners. Google's SRE book defines a **blameless** postmortem as one that focuses on the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, assuming everyone acted with good intentions on the information they had. It traces blameless culture to healthcare and aviation, where mistakes can be fatal, and gives the reason: where people are punished, they stop bringing problems to light.

Questions NIST r2 suggests for the lessons-learned meeting (held within several days of the end of the incident; the SANS handbook suggests within two weeks):

- Exactly what happened, and at what times?
- How well did staff and management perform? Were procedures followed and adequate?
- What information was needed sooner?
- Were any steps taken that might have inhibited recovery?
- What would we do differently next time?
- What corrective actions would prevent similar incidents, and which precursors or indicators should we watch for?
- What tools or resources are missing?

Rev. 3 adds: share lessons as soon as they are identified, not only after recovery, and analyse for **systemic** root causes (RS.AN-03). "An analyst missed an alert" is a contributing factor; "nobody owned unhandled-threat emails from the provider" is systemic.

**A public example: the HSE review.** The HSE board commissioned PwC in June 2021; the 14-week review was published with its full timeline, missed detections, a maturity assessment and prioritised recommendations, such as a central cybersecurity function, an exercised cyber IR plan and recovery planning for a scenario where all IT and communications are down. Publishing it let other health systems learn from it; the US HC3 (Health Sector Cybersecurity Coordination Center) turned it into a lessons-learned brief for American hospitals.

**Tabletop exercises** test plans before a real incident. A facilitator walks the players (incident commander, IT, legal, communications, executives) through a scenario as a series of **injects**, new facts released over time, and asks what they would do, who decides and how they would communicate. Nothing is touched; the output is the gaps. CISA publishes free [Tabletop Exercise Packages](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/services/cisa-tabletop-exercise-packages) with template objectives, scenarios and discussion questions.

blocks.title: A 2-hour ransomware tabletop: injects and what they test

scenes.caption: Inject 1 at minute 0: a ransom note on the file server. Tests paging, declaration and who becomes incident commander.
Minute 20: email and phones are down. Tests the OOB channel and whether the contact list exists outside the encrypted systems.
Minute 45: 40 GB of HR files on a leak site. Tests whether legal knows which notification clocks start and who owns the decision.
Minutes 70 and 90: a journalist calls; backups are 9 days old on offline tape. Tests spokesperson rules, restore priorities and the ransom decision.
Minute 110: the hot wash. Every gap becomes an action with an owner and a date, exactly like a postmortem.

blocks.code:
exercise: "Friday 02:00 ransomware"
objective: test decisions, roles and out-of-band comms, not tools
players: [incident commander, IT ops, legal, comms, CEO]
rules: no blame; "we would check X" is fine, say how and who
injects:
  - t: 0
    say: night shift finds a ransom note on the file server
    ask: who is paged first, and how, if email is down?
  - t: 20
    say: email and the phone system are encrypted too
    ask: where is the contact list? where does the bridge run?
  - t: 45
    say: a leak site lists 40 GB of your HR files
    ask: does this start a regulator clock? whose decision?
  - t: 70
    say: a journalist calls the CEO's mobile
    ask: who speaks, and what can be said yet?
  - t: 90
    say: the newest clean backup is 9 days old, on tape off site
    ask: what do you restore first? who decides on the ransom?
hot_wash:
  - what did we not know that we needed?
  - which decision had no owner?
  - three fixes, each with an owner and a date
blocks.caption: The same exercise as a script for the facilitator. Each inject has one question, so the discussion produces a decision or a visible gap.

blocks.md: Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable. It means the review asks why the system let a reasonable person make that choice, and fixes the system: alert routing, ownership, tooling, training.

**Practise legally.** Only investigate systems and data you own or have written permission to examine.

- [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): free and paid investigation challenges (memory images, disk images, logs).
- [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/): blue-team labs with real artefacts to analyse in your own tools.
- [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/) and [Hack The Box](https://www.hackthebox.com/): both have DFIR and memory-forensics rooms, several free.
- Tools from this course that you can run at home on your own machines: [Volatility 3](https://volatility3.readthedocs.io/en/latest/), [Plaso](https://plaso.readthedocs.io/en/latest/), [Velociraptor](https://docs.velociraptor.app/), [AVML](https://github.com/microsoft/avml), [LiME](https://github.com/504ensicsLabs/LiME), [WinPmem](https://github.com/Velocidex/WinPmem).
- Run a 60-minute tabletop with friends or colleagues using a CISA package.

blocks.question: A postmortem says: "Root cause: the on-call analyst ignored the alert." Why would a blameless review reject this as the conclusion?
options: Because it names a person and stops there; the review should ask why the alert was easy to miss (volume, routing, ownership, monitor mode) and fix that
Because analysts never make mistakes
Because alerts are not part of IR
Because only executives can be named
blocks.explain: Blameless reviews look for systemic causes. If one tired person could miss it, the next one can too; the fix is in the system (alert design, ownership, staffing), which NIST r3 calls the underlying or systemic root cause.

blocks.question: What is the main output of a tabletop exercise?
options: Forensic evidence for court
A certification for the IR team
A list of gaps in plans, roles and communication, each turned into an action with an owner
A restored backup
blocks.explain: Nothing is touched in a tabletop; it tests decisions and coordination. Its value is the gaps it exposes (no OOB contact list, no owner for the ransom decision) and the actions that close them.
